analysis.one_liner: Caps power plant emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide with national limits and emissions trading.
analysis.headline: The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee never took up the bill; it died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have set hard national limits on four pollutants from fossil-fuel power plants — sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide — and let companies trade emission allowances to meet them at lower cost. Starting in 2009 it would also narrow the Clean Air Act's 'new source review' program, which requires old plants to install modern pollution controls when they upgrade, and it would temporarily exempt power plants from some mercury and visibility rules. The bill was sent to the Environment and Public Works Committee and never heard from again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, including communities affected by acid rain, smog, and mercury that settles into lakes and fish. The bill would have required large cuts in all four pollutants and — notably for 2003 — imposed the first-ever mandatory national cap on power-plant carbon dioxide. Public reporting of plant-by-plant emissions would also have improved.

how_it_helps.text: Sets declining national tonnage limits for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury from large fossil-fuel generating units, reaching 2.25 million tons of sulfur dioxide, 1.7 million tons of nitrogen oxides, and 10 tons of mercury per year by 2013 and after [S3].
Establishes the first mandatory national cap on power-plant carbon dioxide, holding emissions to projected 2006 levels from 2009 and to 2001 levels from 2013 onward, with a trading program [S3].

Requires quarterly emissions monitoring and reporting and makes emissions data for every covered plant available to the public, with penalties of $5,000 per excess ton of nitrogen oxides, $10,000 per pound of mercury, and $100 per ton of carbon dioxide [S3].
Directs NOAA to provide regional air-quality forecasts and warnings for ten regions of the country [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired power plant owners would bear the cost of cutting emissions or buying allowances, costs that could be passed to electricity customers. Coal producers would face lower demand if carbon dioxide limits pushed utilities toward natural gas, nuclear, and renewables.

drawbacks.text: From 2009 the bill would narrow the new source review program so that existing plants no longer need pre-construction permits for changes unless the maximum hourly emission rate rises, would let cost be considered in setting the lowest achievable emission rate, and would spare new plants in nonattainment areas from buying emission offsets [S3].

It would exempt affected power plants from Clean Air Act hazardous air pollutant requirements for mercury for eight years and from visibility-protection requirements for twenty years, replacing those rules with the new tonnage caps [S3].
Allowance trading means some plants can keep polluting by buying permits from cleaner ones, and allocations of allowances to existing plants could not be challenged in court [S3].
The carbon dioxide cap was set at roughly 2001 emissions levels from 2013, far shallower than what climate science-based proposals of the era called for.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real public-health gains — deep cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and the first mandatory carbon dioxide cap on power plants — in exchange for costs to coal-heavy utilities and their customers. But it bought utility cooperation by loosening parts of the existing Clean Air Act: new source review would shrink after 2009, mercury rules would be supplanted for years, and old plants' allowances could not be challenged in court. Environmental advocates at the time saw it as far better than the Bush administration's competing 'Clear Skies' plan but weaker in places than enforcing the existing law. On balance it would likely have produced cleaner air than what actually happened in the following years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never held a markup or vote, and it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

narrative.text: Sen. Thomas Carper introduced the bill on April 9, 2003 with three Republican cosponsors [S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works the same day — the only action it ever received [S5].
No committee markup, floor vote, or further action ever followed before the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal-burning power plant owners and coal producers came out ahead: without a vote, no mandatory carbon dioxide cap or deeper mercury and sulfur dioxide limits were ever imposed, and the Bush administration's preference for voluntary carbon reductions and lighter-touch rules prevailed for the rest of the Congress.

for.name: Sen. Thomas R. Carper
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, a four-pollutant cap-and-trade compromise, and referred it to the Environment and Public Works Committee.

for.name: 3 of 51 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Sen. James Inhofe
against.role: Chair, Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill during the entire two-year Congress.

against.name: President George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory carbon dioxide caps, backed a voluntary approach, and promoted the competing Clear Skies proposal, which set no mandatory CO2 limit.

against.name: Coal-burning electric utilities and coal producers
against.role: Power plant owners and coal industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandatory carbon dioxide limits and lobbied against four-pollutant cap legislation during the 108th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Democrat and three Republicans — but with no votes ever held, the only decisive actor was the Republican committee chairman, who never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have imposed binding caps and penalties on their sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide emissions, but it also handed them free allowances, relaxed new source review from 2009, and promised twenty years of regulatory stability. Because the bill died, they avoided all of the caps entirely.

Mandatory carbon dioxide caps and deep sulfur dioxide cuts would have reduced demand for coal in electricity generation, accelerating a shift toward natural gas, nuclear, and renewables. Blocking the bill preserved coal's market position.

The bill would have given free carbon dioxide allowances to incremental nuclear generation and reserved allowances for new renewable energy units, rewarding zero-carbon electricity. Its defeat delayed that advantage.
Carbon dioxide and mercury caps fall hardest on coal, making gas-fired generation relatively more competitive. Its defeat kept coal relatively advantaged.
